l: Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians / Chapter 1
s: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by God's will, greets the saints at Ephesus and the faithful in Christ Jesus with grace and peace. He blesses God the Father for choosing believers before the world's foundation, predestining them for adoption, and granting redemption and forgiveness through Christ's blood. God has made known the mystery of his will: to sum up all things in Christ, and believers have received an inheritance and have been sealed with the promised Holy Spirit as a pledge. Paul says he gives thanks and prays for the Ephesians because of their faith in the Lord Jesus and love for all the saints, asking that God give them a spirit of wisdom and revelation. He describes God's power as the power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him at God's right hand, far above every rule and name, with all things under his feet and him as head over all things for the assembly, which is his body.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians / Chapter 1
s: Paul identifies himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus through God's will and writes to the saints at Ephesus. He gives thanks for them, mentions them in his prayers, and asks that God give them a spirit of wisdom and revelation, enlightened hearts, and knowledge of the hope of his calling.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians / Chapter 1
s: God, the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, is blessed for blessing believers with every spiritual blessing in Christ. He chose them before the world's foundation, predestined them for adoption, made known the mystery of his will, sealed believers with the Holy Spirit, and worked his mighty power in Christ by raising him from the dead.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians / Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is the one in whom believers are chosen, redeemed through his blood, forgiven, and given an inheritance, and in whom all things in heaven and on earth are to be summed up. God raised him from the dead, seated him at his right hand far above all rule and authority, put all things under his feet, and made him head over all things for the assembly, his body.

l: saints, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians / Chapter 1
s: The saints at Ephesus, called faithful in Christ Jesus, are greeted with grace and peace. Paul has heard of their faith in the Lord Jesus and their love toward all the saints; having heard the word of truth and believed, they were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.

l: the readers (believers addressed), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians / Chapter 1
s: Believers, referred to as "us" and "we," were blessed with every spiritual blessing, chosen to be holy and without defect in love, and given redemption, forgiveness, and an inheritance in Christ. They were foreordained to be to the praise of God's glory, and the Holy Spirit is a pledge of their inheritance.

l: predestination and adoption, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians / Chapter 1
s: God predestined believers for adoption as children through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his desire. This is linked to his choosing them before the foundation of the world and is said to be to the praise of the glory of his grace.

l: Christ's resurrection and exaltation, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians / Chapter 1
s: God worked his mighty strength in Christ by raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand in the heavenly places. This places him far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name, in this age and the one to come, with all things in subjection under his feet.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 tells the readers that God, rich in mercy and love, made them alive together with Christ when they were dead in transgressions and sins, raised them up and seated them with him in the heavenly places. It says they are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and are God's workmanship created in Christ Jesus for good works. It then reminds the Gentiles that they were once separate from Christ, alienated from Israel and without hope, but are now brought near by the blood of Christ. Christ is described as their peace, who broke down the middle wall, abolished the hostility, made one new man of two, and reconciled both to God through the cross. The Gentiles are now fellow citizens and members of God's household, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus as chief cornerstone, growing into a holy temple and habitation of God in the Spirit.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 2
s: Christ Jesus is the one with whom God made believers alive, raised them up and seated them in the heavenly places. He is called our peace: he made both one, broke down the middle wall, abolished the hostility in his flesh, and reconciled both to God through the cross. He preached peace to those far and near, and is the chief cornerstone of the building.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 2
s: God, rich in mercy and great love, made those dead in trespasses alive together with Christ, raised them and seated them with him. He gave salvation as a gift and prepared good works beforehand for his people to walk in. He is the one to whom both groups are reconciled, with access through one Spirit to the Father, and his habitation is the building being built together.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 2
s: The Gentiles, called "uncircumcision," were once separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, without hope and without God in the world. Now they are made near in the blood of Christ and are no longer strangers and foreigners but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household.

l: grace, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 2
s: Grace is the means by which believers have been saved, stated twice in the chapter. It is tied to God's kindness toward us in Christ Jesus, whose exceeding riches he will show in the ages to come.

l: salvation through faith, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 2
s: The text says believers have been saved by grace through faith, and that this is not of themselves but the gift of God. It is not of works, so that no one would boast.

l: peace, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 2
s: Peace is identified with Christ himself, who made both groups one and broke down the dividing wall. He abolished the hostility and the law of commandments in ordinances to make peace, and he preached peace to those far off and those near.

l: holy temple, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 2
s: The holy temple is the whole building, fitted together and growing in the Lord, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus as chief cornerstone. The readers are built together in him as a habitation of God in the Spirit.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 3
s: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of the Gentiles, explains that by revelation God made known to him the mystery of Christ, which was hidden in past generations but is now revealed to the apostles and prophets. The mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the Good News. Paul was made a servant of this Good News by God's grace, to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ and, through the assembly, make God's manifold wisdom known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places. He asks the readers not to lose heart at his troubles, then bows his knees to the Father and prays that they be strengthened, that Christ dwell in their hearts, that they know Christ's love, and be filled with the fullness of God. The chapter ends with a doxology giving glory to God in the assembly and in Christ Jesus forever.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 3
s: Paul identifies himself as the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of the Gentiles, and says the mystery was made known to him by revelation. He was made a servant of the Good News by God's grace and power, calls himself the very least of all saints, and was given grace to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ to the Gentiles. He asks the readers not to lose heart at his troubles and bows his knees to the Father in prayer for them.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 3
s: Jesus Christ is the one whose prisoner Paul is, and the one through whom God created all things. God accomplished his eternal purpose in him, and in him believers have boldness and access in confidence through faith. Paul prays that Christ may dwell in the readers' hearts through faith and that they may know his love, which surpasses knowledge; glory is given to God in Christ Jesus to all generations.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 3
s: God gave grace to Paul, revealed the mystery to him, and kept it hidden for ages in himself as the creator of all things through Jesus Christ. His manifold wisdom is made known through the assembly to the principalities and powers, according to the eternal purpose he accomplished in Christ Jesus. He is addressed as the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, and as one able to do exceedingly abundantly above all we ask or think.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 3
s: The Gentiles are declared to be fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of God's promise in Christ Jesus through the Good News. Paul is a prisoner on their behalf, and was given grace to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ to them. Paul says his troubles for them are their glory.

l: mystery of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 3
s: The mystery of Christ was made known to Paul by revelation, and he had written of it before in few words so readers could perceive his understanding of it. It was not made known to earlier generations but has now been revealed to God's holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit. Its content is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the body, and partakers of the promise, and it had been hidden for ages in God.

l: grace, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 3
s: The grace of God was given to Paul toward the Gentiles as an administration, and by it he was made a servant of the Good News according to the working of God's power. It was given to the very least of all saints so that he might preach the unsearchable riches of Christ.

l: assembly, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 3
s: The assembly is the means through which the manifold wisdom of God is now made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places. The chapter closes by giving glory to God in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever.

l: Paul's prayer for the readers, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 3
s: Paul bows his knees to the Father and asks that, according to the riches of his glory, the readers be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person. He prays that Christ dwell in their hearts through faith, that they be rooted and grounded in love, and that they comprehend with all the saints the width, length, height and depth. He also prays that they know Christ's love, which surpasses knowledge, and be filled with all the fullness of God.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: In this chapter the prisoner in the Lord urges the readers to walk worthily of their calling with humility, patience, and love, keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, since there is one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all. Christ, who descended and ascended above all the heavens, gave grace and gifts, including apostles, prophets, evangelists, and shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints and build up the body until all attain unity and the full stature of Christ. The readers are told to stop being children tossed by false doctrine, to speak truth in love, and to grow into Christ the head. They are also told not to walk as the Gentiles do, darkened and hardened in heart, but to put away the old man, be renewed in mind, and put on the new man created in righteousness and holiness. Practical commands follow: speak truth, be angry without sinning, stop stealing and labor, avoid corrupt speech, not grieve the Holy Spirit, put away bitterness and malice, and forgive as God in Christ forgave them.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: Identifying himself as the prisoner in the Lord, he begs the readers to walk worthily of their calling. He testifies in the Lord that they must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, and he gives them instructions for putting off the old life and living in love and truth.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: Christ ascended on high, leading captivity captive and giving gifts to people, having first descended into the lower parts of the earth, and he fills all things. He is the head into whom the body grows, the measure of fullness the believers are to reach, and the one in whom God forgave them.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: God is described as the one God and Father of all, who is over all, through all, and in all. The new man is created in his likeness, and he forgave the readers in Christ, which is the pattern for their forgiveness of one another.

l: Holy Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: The Holy Spirit is the one Spirit of the one body, whose unity the readers are to keep in the bond of peace. They are told not to grieve him, since in him they were sealed for the day of redemption.

l: the readers (believers addressed), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: The readers are urged to walk worthily of their calling with humility, patience, and love, and to grow into maturity rather than be tossed about by false doctrine. They are told to put away the old man, be renewed in mind, put on the new man, and abandon falsehood, theft, corrupt speech, bitterness, and malice in favor of truth, honest labor, kindness, and forgiveness.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: The Gentiles are described as walking in the futility of their mind, darkened in understanding and alienated from the life of God through ignorance and hardness of heart. Having become callous, they gave themselves up to lust and uncleanness with greediness, and the readers are told not to walk as they do.

l: the church (body of Christ), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: The body of Christ is one, and is built up through the work of serving until all attain unity of faith and knowledge of the Son of God. Christ the head fits and knits it together through what every joint supplies, so that it increases and builds itself up in love.

l: church leaders (apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: Christ gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some shepherds and teachers. Their purpose is the perfecting of the saints, the work of serving, and the building up of the body of Christ.

l: unity of the Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: The readers are urged to be eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. It rests on the one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all.

l: old man, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: The old man is the former way of life, which grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit. The readers are told to put it away.

l: new man, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
s: The new man is to be put on by the readers as they are renewed in the spirit of their mind. He has been created in the likeness of God in righteousness and holiness of truth.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 5
s: The chapter urges its readers to imitate God and walk in love as Christ loved and gave himself up for them. It warns against sexual immorality, uncleanness, covetousness, filthy talk and deceptive words, saying such people have no inheritance in the Kingdom of Christ and God and that God's wrath comes on the disobedient. It contrasts the readers' former darkness with their present life as light in the Lord, calling them to reprove the deeds of darkness, wake from sleep, live wisely, and be filled with the Spirit rather than drunk with wine. It then gives household instructions: wives are to be subject to their husbands as the assembly is to Christ, and husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the assembly, sanctifying her and presenting her holy. The chapter closes by tying marriage to the mystery of Christ and the assembly and telling each husband to love his wife and each wife to respect her husband.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 5
s: Christ is presented as the model of love, having loved the readers and given himself up for them as an offering and sacrifice to God. He is head of the assembly and savior of the body, and he sanctified the assembly by cleansing her with the washing of water with the word so he could present her gloriously holy and without defect. He will shine on those who awake from sleep and arise from the dead, and the passage's mystery of one flesh is said to concern him and the assembly.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 5
s: God is the one the readers are to imitate as beloved children, and the one to whom Christ's sacrifice was offered as a sweet-smelling fragrance. His wrath comes on the children of disobedience because of sexual immorality, uncleanness and covetousness, and his Kingdom, shared with Christ, is not inherited by such people. The readers are to give thanks always to God, even the Father, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.

l: the church (body of Christ), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 5
s: The assembly is described as being subject to Christ, who is its head and savior. Christ loved it and gave himself up for her, cleansing and sanctifying her so that he might present her to himself gloriously, without spot, wrinkle or defect. The Lord nourishes and cherishes the assembly, and the readers are members of his body, of his flesh and bones.

l: husbands, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 5
s: Husbands are commanded to love their wives as Christ loved the assembly and gave himself up for her, and to love them as their own bodies. The text says that a husband who loves his wife loves himself, that he is head of the wife as Christ is head of the assembly, and that each must love his wife as himself.

l: wives, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 5
s: Wives are told to be subject to their own husbands as to the Lord, in everything, just as the assembly is subject to Christ. The chapter ends by saying the wife must see that she respects her husband. The husband-wife union is linked to the one-flesh passage and to the mystery concerning Christ and the assembly.

l: sexual immorality and uncleanness, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 5
s: Sexual immorality, all uncleanness and covetousness are not even to be mentioned among the saints, and filthiness, foolish talking and jesting are also ruled out. The text says no sexually immoral or unclean person, nor covetous person (an idolater), has an inheritance in the Kingdom of Christ and God. Because of these things God's wrath comes on the children of disobedience, so the readers must not partner with those who practice them.

l: light and darkness, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 5
s: The readers were once darkness but are now light in the Lord, and are told to walk as children of light, whose fruit is goodness, righteousness and truth. They are to have no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness but to reprove them, since the things done in secret are shameful even to mention. Everything reproved is revealed by the light, for everything that reveals is light, and Christ will shine on those who awake from sleep.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: Chapter 6 first gives household instructions: children are to obey and honor their parents, fathers are not to provoke their children, servants are to serve their masters sincerely as to Christ, and masters are to stop threatening because they share a Master in heaven who shows no partiality. It then urges readers to be strong in the Lord and put on the whole armor of God to stand against the devil's wiles and the spiritual forces of wickedness. The armor consists of the belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, preparation of the Good News of peace on the feet, shield of faith, helmet of salvation, and sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, along with prayer for all the saints. Paul asks for prayer that he may boldly make known the mystery of the Good News as an ambassador in chains. He says he is sending Tychicus to report on his affairs and comfort the readers, and closes with blessings of peace, love, faith, and grace.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: Paul urges his readers to be strong in the Lord and to put on the whole armor of God. He asks them to pray that he may speak boldly about the mystery of the Good News, describing himself as an ambassador in chains. He sends Tychicus to inform and comfort them, and closes with blessings of peace and grace.

l: Tychicus, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: Tychicus is called the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord. Paul sends him to the readers to make known all about Paul's affairs and state and to comfort their hearts.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: The Lord Jesus Christ is the one whom servants serve and obey as to Christ, and the source, together with God the Father, of peace and love with faith. Grace is wished upon all who love him with incorruptible love.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: God is the one whose will servants do from the heart and whose armor believers are to put on. He is called the Father, a source of peace and love with faith, and his word is the sword of the Spirit.

l: children, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: Children are told to obey their parents in the Lord, because this is right. They are to honor father and mother, the first commandment with a promise of well-being and long life on the earth.

l: parents, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: Parents are to be obeyed and honored by their children. Fathers are told not to provoke their children to wrath but to nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

l: servants, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: Servants are told to obey their earthly masters with fear and trembling and singleness of heart, as to Christ. They should serve from the heart and not merely when watched, knowing the Lord will repay whatever good each does, whether bound or free.

l: masters, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: Masters are told to do the same things toward their servants and to give up threatening. They are reminded that their Master, who is also the servants' Master, is in heaven and shows no partiality.

l: the devil, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: The devil is described as using wiles against which believers must stand. The armor of God is put on so they can stand against these wiles.

l: spiritual authorities (powers over which Christ rules), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: The spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places are named alongside the principalities, powers, and world's rulers of the darkness of this age. They are the true opponents of believers, whose wrestling is not against flesh and blood.

l: armor of God, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
s: The armor of God is to be put on whole so believers can withstand in the evil day and stand. It comprises the belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, feet fitted with the preparation of the Good News of peace, shield of faith that quenches the fiery darts of the evil one, helmet of salvation, and sword of the Spirit.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 1
s: Paul, writing with Timothy, greets the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi along with the overseers and servants, and thanks God for their partnership in the Good News. He prays that their love will abound in knowledge and discernment so they may be sincere and filled with the fruits of righteousness. Paul explains that his bonds have advanced the Good News, becoming known to the palace guard and emboldening most of the brothers, while some preach Christ from envy and others from good will, and he rejoices that Christ is proclaimed either way. He is torn between dying to be with Christ, which is far better, and remaining in the flesh for the Philippians' sake, and he expects to remain. He urges them to live worthily of the Good News, stand firm in one spirit, and not be frightened by adversaries, since they have been granted both belief and suffering on Christ's behalf.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 1
s: Paul, with Timothy, writes to the saints at Philippi, thanking God for them and praying that their love abounds. He says his bonds have advanced the Good News, that he rejoices whenever Christ is proclaimed, and that he is hard pressed between desiring to depart and be with Christ and remaining for their progress and joy. He expects to remain and urges them to live worthily and stand firm.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is named as a source of grace and peace, and Paul and Timothy are his servants. Paul says his bonds are in Christ, that Christ is proclaimed from both envy and good will, and that Christ will be magnified in Paul's body by life or death. Departing to be with Christ is called far better, and the Philippians are granted to believe in him and suffer on his behalf.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 1
s: God is called Father and is the one Paul thanks whenever he remembers the Philippians. He began a good work in them and will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ, and he is Paul's witness to Paul's longing for them. The fruits of righteousness are to the glory and praise of God, and the brothers speak his word without fear.

l: Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 1
s: The saints at Philippi, with their overseers and servants, are greeted and thanked for their partnership in the Good News from the first day until now. They are partakers with Paul of grace in his bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the Good News. They are urged to live worthily, stand firm in one spirit with one soul, not be frightened by adversaries, and are told they share the same conflict Paul has.

l: Good News, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 1
s: The Good News is furthered by the Philippians' partnership, and Paul's circumstances have turned out to its progress. Paul is appointed for its defense, and some preach Christ from envy and some from good will, yet Christ is proclaimed either way. The Philippians are told to let their way of life be worthy of it and to strive together for its faith.

l: Paul's imprisonment, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 1
s: Paul's bonds became evident to the whole palace guard and all the rest as being in Christ. They made most of the brothers more confident and bold to speak the word of God without fear, though some preach from selfish ambition thinking to add affliction to his chains. Paul trusts they will turn out to his salvation through the Philippians' prayers and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.

l: life and death, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 1
s: Paul says that to him to live is Christ and to die is gain, and that Christ will be magnified in his body whether by life or by death. He is hard pressed between the two, since departing to be with Christ is far better but remaining in the flesh brings fruit and is more needful for the Philippians. He concludes that he will remain for their progress and joy in the faith.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 2
s: In this chapter the author urges the Philippian believers to be united, humble, and concerned for others, holding up Christ Jesus as the model. Christ, existing in the form of God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to death on the cross, after which God exalted him so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess him as Lord. The author tells the believers to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, noting that God works in them, and to act without complaining so they shine as lights in a crooked generation. He says he is glad even if poured out as a sacrifice for their faith. He hopes to send Timothy soon, praising his proven service, and is sending Epaphroditus, who nearly died for Christ's work, asking that they receive him with joy and honor.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 2
s: Jesus Christ is presented as the model of mindset: existing in the form of God, he did not grasp at equality with God but emptied himself, took a servant's form, and was made in human likeness. He humbled himself to the point of death on the cross, and God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 2
s: God highly exalted Jesus and gave him the name above every name, so that every knee should bow and every tongue confess Jesus Christ as Lord to the glory of God the Father. God works in the believers both to will and to work for his good pleasure, and he had mercy on Epaphroditus and on Paul by sparing Epaphroditus from death.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 2
s: Paul asks the believers to make his joy full through unity and humility, and says he is glad even if poured out as a sacrifice for their faith. He hopes to send Timothy soon and to come himself shortly, and he is sending Epaphroditus back to them, hoping to have reason to boast on the day of Christ that he did not run or labor in vain.

l: Timothy, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 2
s: Timothy is the one Paul hopes to send soon, saying he has no one else like-minded who will truly care for the Philippians, since others seek their own interests. He has proved himself, serving with Paul like a child serving a father in furthering the Good News.

l: Epaphroditus, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 2
s: Epaphroditus is described by Paul as brother, fellow worker, fellow soldier, and the Philippians' apostle and servant of Paul's need. He was sick nearly to death but God had mercy on him; he longed for the Philippians and was troubled that they had heard of his illness. Paul sends him back so they may rejoice, and asks that they receive him with joy and honor him, since he risked his life for Christ's work to supply what was lacking in their service to Paul.

l: Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 2
s: The Philippian believers are exhorted to be like-minded, humble, and attentive to others' interests, and to work out their salvation with fear and trembling. They are told to avoid complaining and arguing so they may be blameless children of God shining as lights and holding up the word of life. They are praised for having always obeyed, and are asked to rejoice with Paul and to welcome Epaphroditus honorably.

l: humility and unity, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 2
s: Paul calls for being of one mind, one accord, and the same love, doing nothing from rivalry or conceit but counting others better than oneself and looking to others' interests. Christ's example is held up as the pattern, and the believers are further told to act without complaining and arguing.

l: Christ's self-emptying and exaltation, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 2
s: The text describes Christ emptying himself, taking a servant's form, being found in human form, and becoming obedient to death on a cross. This is followed by God's exaltation of him, giving him the name above every name, with universal bowing in heaven, on earth, and under the earth and confession that Jesus Christ is Lord.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: In Chapter 3 the writer, who is Paul, urges his brothers to rejoice in the Lord and warns them against the dogs, the evil workers, and the false circumcision. He lists his own credentials in the flesh, including circumcision on the eighth day, the tribe of Benjamin, being a Pharisee, and being found blameless under the law, but counts them all a loss for the sake of Christ. He desires a righteousness from God through faith, to know Christ, the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, and to attain the resurrection from the dead. Paul says he has not yet obtained it but presses on toward the goal for the prize of God's high calling in Christ Jesus, and he asks the brothers to imitate him. He contrasts those who live as enemies of the cross, whose end is destruction, with believers whose citizenship is in heaven, where Christ will change their bodies to be like his glorious body.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: Paul calls his brothers to rejoice and lists his fleshly credentials: circumcised the eighth day, of Israel and Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, a persecutor of the assembly, and blameless under the law. He counts all of it a loss for Christ, says he has not yet obtained or been made perfect, and presses on toward the goal while urging others to imitate him.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: Christ Jesus is the one Paul counts all things loss for, desiring to gain him, be found in him, and know the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings. He took hold of Paul, and as the Savior and Lord from heaven he will change the body of humiliation to be conformed to his glorious body, by the working through which he can subject all things to himself.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: God is worshiped in the Spirit by those who are the true circumcision. He is the source of the righteousness that comes by faith, will reveal to the readers anything in which they think otherwise, and has issued the high calling in Christ Jesus.

l: Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: The brothers are told to rejoice in the Lord, to beware of the dogs, evil workers, and false circumcision, and to be imitators of Paul together. They are urged to walk by the same rule and be of the same mind, and are told their citizenship is in heaven, where they wait for a Savior.

l: enemies of the cross of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: Paul says many walk as enemies of the cross of Christ, and he tells of them now even weeping. Their end is destruction, their god is the belly, their glory is in their shame, and they think about earthly things.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: The law is the standard under which Paul was a Pharisee and was found blameless in the righteousness which is in the law. He counts that righteousness as not his own basis for standing, preferring the righteousness through faith in Christ.

l: righteousness, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: Paul distinguishes the righteousness of the law, which he once had and found blameless, from the righteousness which is from God by faith in Christ. He wants to be found in Christ not having a righteousness of his own, but the one from God through faith.

l: resurrection, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: Paul wants to know the power of Christ's resurrection and hopes by any means to attain the resurrection from the dead. He also expects Christ to change the body of humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory.

l: the goal and prize of the high calling, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 3
s: Paul presses on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. He says he has not yet taken hold of it, but forgets what lies behind and stretches forward to what is ahead.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: In Chapter 4, the author urges the beloved brothers to stand firm in the Lord and exhorts Euodia and Syntyche to think the same way, asking a true partner to help them. He commands the readers to rejoice always, be gentle, avoid anxiety by praying with thanksgiving, and think on whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report, promising that the peace of God will guard their hearts. He thanks the Philippians for reviving their concern for him, explaining that he has learned to be content in every circumstance and can do all things through Christ who strengthens him. He recalls that they alone shared with him in giving and receiving, even in Thessalonica, and that through Epaphroditus he received their gift as a pleasing sacrifice to God. He promises that God will supply every need of theirs, and closes with glory to God, greetings from the brothers and all the saints, especially Caesar's household, and a blessing of grace.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: Paul exhorts Euodia and Syntyche, asks a true partner to help them, and commands the readers to rejoice, avoid anxiety, and think on good things. He says he has learned contentment in every state, can do all things through Christ who strengthens him, and has received the Philippians' gift through Epaphroditus, seeking the fruit to their account rather than the gift itself.

l: Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: The Philippians are told to stand firm in the Lord, rejoice always, pray rather than be anxious, and practice what they learned from Paul. They are praised for reviving their thought for him, sharing in his affliction, and being the only assembly to share in giving and receiving with him, even sending to his need in Thessalonica.

l: Euodia, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: Euodia is exhorted by name to think the same way in the Lord. She is among the women who labored with Paul in the Good News.

l: Syntyche, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: Syntyche is exhorted by name to think the same way in the Lord. She is among the women who labored with Paul in the Good News.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: The peace of God guards hearts and thoughts in Christ Jesus, and God's riches are given in Christ Jesus. Paul says he can do all things through Christ who strengthens him, and the chapter closes with a prayer that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: God is described as the source of peace that surpasses all understanding and as the God of peace who will be with those who practice what Paul taught. He will supply every need of the Philippians according to his riches in glory, receives their gift as an acceptable sacrifice, and is given glory forever.

l: gift from the Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: The gift was brought by Epaphroditus and received by Paul, who calls it a sweet-smelling fragrance and an acceptable, well-pleasing sacrifice to God. Paul says he does not seek the gift itself but the fruit that increases to the Philippians' account, and he notes they had also sent aid more than once in Thessalonica.

l: rejoicing, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: Paul commands the readers to rejoice in the Lord always and repeats the command. He himself rejoices greatly in the Lord that the Philippians have revived their thought for him.

l: contentment, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, Chapter 4
s: Paul says he has learned to be content in whatever state he is in, knowing how to be humbled and how to abound, to be filled and to be hungry. He ties this ability to Christ who strengthens him, and says he does not speak out of lack.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 1
s: Paul and Timothy greet the saints and faithful brothers at Colossae and give thanks for their faith in Christ Jesus, their love for all the saints, and their hope, which they learned from Epaphras. Paul prays that they be filled with the knowledge of God's will, walk worthily, bear fruit, and be strengthened with joy. He describes how God delivered believers from the power of darkness into the Kingdom of his Son, in whom there is redemption and forgiveness of sins. The Son is portrayed as the image of the invisible God, firstborn of all creation, through whom and for whom all things were created, head of the assembly, and the one through whom all things are reconciled through the blood of his cross. Paul then says the Colossians, once alienated, are now reconciled if they continue in the faith, and he rejoices in his sufferings as a servant of the assembly, proclaiming the once-hidden mystery, Christ in you, the hope of glory.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 1
s: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by God's will, writes with Timothy to the saints at Colossae, giving thanks and praying constantly for them. He rejoices in his sufferings for their sake and says he was made a servant of the Good News and of the assembly, entrusted with the stewardship to fulfill the word of God. He labors, admonishing and teaching every man, to present everyone perfect in Christ, striving according to Christ's working in him.

l: Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is described as the Son of God's love, in whom believers have redemption and forgiveness of sins. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, before all things, who holds all things together, and the head of the body, the assembly, and the firstborn from the dead. All things were created through him and for him, and through the blood of his cross he made peace and reconciles all things to himself.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 1
s: God is called Father of the Lord Jesus Christ and is thanked for making believers fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light. He delivered them from the power of darkness and translated them into the Kingdom of his Son. All the fullness was pleased to dwell in the Son, and God was pleased to make known the riches of the glory of the mystery among the Gentiles.

l: recipients of the letter (Colossians), Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 1
s: The believers at Colossae are praised for their faith in Christ Jesus and love toward all the saints, having learned the grace of God in truth from Epaphras. They were once alienated and enemies in mind through evil deeds but are now reconciled through Christ's death, to be presented holy, without defect and blameless, if they continue grounded and steadfast in the faith. Paul prays that they be filled with knowledge of God's will, walk worthily, and bear fruit.

l: Good News, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 1
s: The Good News carries the word of the truth and the hope laid up in the heavens, and it has come to the Colossians. It is bearing fruit and growing in all the world, as it does in them, and it was proclaimed in all creation under heaven. Paul was made a servant of it.

l: mystery of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 1
s: The mystery was hidden for ages and generations but has now been revealed to God's saints. God was pleased to make known its glorious riches among the Gentiles, and it is identified as Christ in you, the hope of glory. Paul and his companions proclaim Christ, teaching every man in all wisdom.

l: redemption and reconciliation, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 1
s: In the Son believers have redemption, the forgiveness of sins, and have been delivered from the power of darkness into his Kingdom. Through him God reconciles all things to himself, whether on earth or in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross. The Colossians, once alienated, have been reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to be presented holy and blameless.

l: creation, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 1
s: All things in the heavens and on the earth, visible and invisible, including thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, were created by, through and for the Son. He is before all things and in him all things are held together. The Son is called firstborn of all creation, and the Good News has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: In this chapter the author says he struggles for the Colossians, for those at Laodicea, and for others who have not seen him, so that their hearts may be comforted and they may know the mystery of God and of Christ, in whom all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. He urges the recipients to keep walking in Christ as they received him, and warns them not to be robbed by philosophy, vain deceit, and the tradition of men. He explains that in Christ the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, that they were circumcised, buried, and raised with him, and that God made them alive and forgave their trespasses. The handwriting in ordinances against them was wiped out and nailed to the cross, and Christ stripped the principalities and powers and triumphed over them. On this basis the author tells them not to let anyone judge them over food, drink, feast days, new moons, or Sabbaths, nor rob them through self-abasement and angel worship, and he questions why those who died with Christ submit to rules such as 'Don't handle, nor taste, nor touch'.

l: Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: Christ is the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden and in whom all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily. He is the head of all principality and power, and he triumphed over the principalities and powers. The recipients are to walk in him, are made full in him, and are told to hold firmly to him as the Head, from whom the whole body grows.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: God raised Christ from the dead and works through faith to raise believers with him. He made the recipients alive together with Christ, forgave all trespasses, and caused the body to grow with 'God's growth'. The mystery of God is described as being of the Father and of Christ.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: The author says he struggles greatly for the Colossians, for those at Laodicea, and for others who have not seen his face. Though absent in the flesh, he is with them in spirit, rejoicing to see their order and the steadfastness of their faith. He warns them against being deluded or robbed by persuasive speech, philosophy, and human rules.

l: recipients of the letter (Colossians), Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: The recipients are urged to walk in Christ, rooted, built up, established in the faith, and abounding in thanksgiving. They were circumcised in Christ, buried and raised with him in baptism, and made alive after being dead in trespasses. They are warned against philosophy, judgment over observances, angel worship, and submitting to ordinances although they died with Christ from the elemental spirits of the world.

l: principalities and powers, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: Christ is the head of all principality and power. In this unit they are stripped by Christ, who made an open show of them and triumphed over them in the cross.

l: false teachers (anyone who robs you), Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: These unnamed people are warned against as ones who might delude the recipients with persuasive speech, rob them through philosophy and vain deceit, judge them over food and festivals, or rob them of their prize. One such person is described as dwelling in things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind, and not holding firmly to the Head.

l: handwriting in ordinances, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: The handwriting in ordinances was against 'us' and is described as wiped out. God has taken it out of the way by nailing it to the cross.

l: philosophy and tradition of men, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: Philosophy and vain deceit, according to the tradition of men and the elemental spirits of the world and not according to Christ, are what the recipients must guard against being robbed by. The precepts and doctrines of men are said to appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body, but to have no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

l: dietary and festival observances, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 2
s: Eating, drinking, feast days, new moons, and Sabbath days are things for which the recipients are told to let no one judge them. They are called a shadow of things to come, while the body is Christ's. Rules such as 'Don't handle, nor taste, nor touch' are said to concern things that perish with use.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 addresses readers who have been raised together with Christ, urging them to seek and set their minds on things above, since they died and their life is hidden with Christ in God. It commands them to put to death earthly vices such as sexual immorality, anger, malice, slander, and lying, because God's wrath comes on the disobedient. It describes putting off the old man and putting on the new man, who is renewed after the image of his Creator, where Christ is all and in all. The readers are told to put on compassion, kindness, humility, forgiveness, and love, to let the peace of God rule and the word of Christ dwell richly, and to do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus. The chapter ends with instructions to wives, husbands, children, fathers, and servants, noting that the wrongdoer will be repaid and there is no partiality.

l: Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: Christ is described as seated on the right hand of God and as the readers' life, who will be revealed in glory with them. He forgave the readers, serving as the model for their forgiveness of each other, and he is all and in all. The readers are to do everything in his name and serve him as Lord.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: God is the one at whose right hand Christ is seated, and his wrath comes on the children of disobedience because of the listed vices. He has chosen the readers as holy and beloved, his peace is to rule their hearts, and the readers give thanks to him as Father through Jesus. He shows no partiality.

l: recipients of the letter (Colossians), Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: The readers are told they were raised with Christ, died, and have their life hidden with Christ in God, and will be revealed with him in glory. They are commanded to seek things above, put to death earthly vices, put off the old man, put on the new man and the Christian virtues, and walk in love. They are also to be thankful, let Christ's word dwell in them, teach and admonish one another with songs, and do all in the Lord Jesus' name.

l: old man, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: The old man is something the readers have put off, along with his doings, which include lying. He is contrasted with the new man.

l: new man, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: The new man is what the readers have put on, and he is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator. In this new state there is no distinction between Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, bondservant, or free, because Christ is all and in all.

l: vices of earthly nature, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: The members on the earth are listed as sexual immorality, uncleanness, depraved passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry, and the readers must put them to death. Further vices to put away are anger, wrath, malice, slander, shameful speaking, and lying. God's wrath comes on the children of disobedience for these things, in which the readers once walked.

l: Christian virtues, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: The readers are to put on a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance, bearing with and forgiving each other as Christ forgave them. Love is placed above all of these as the bond of perfection. Peace of God, thankfulness, and the word of Christ dwelling richly are also commended.

l: wives, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: Wives are told to be in subjection to their husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

l: husbands, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: Husbands are told to love their wives and not be bitter against them.

l: children, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: Children are told to obey their parents in all things, because this pleases the Lord.

l: fathers, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: Fathers are told not to provoke their children, so that the children won't be discouraged.

l: servants, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 3
s: Servants are told to obey their masters according to the flesh in all things, not just when watched, but in singleness of heart, fearing God. They are to work heartily as for the Lord, knowing they will receive the reward of the inheritance from the Lord Christ, whom they serve. The one who does wrong will be repaid, with no partiality.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 closes the letter with final instructions and greetings. Paul tells masters to treat servants justly, urges the recipients to persevere in prayer, including for his own opportunity to speak the mystery of Christ, and to walk wisely toward outsiders with gracious speech. He says Tychicus and Onesimus are being sent to report on his affairs and to comfort the recipients' hearts. Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus called Justus, Epaphras, Luke and Demas send greetings, and Paul asks that the Laodiceans be greeted and that letters be exchanged between the two assemblies. He tells Archippus to fulfill his ministry and signs the letter with his own hand, asking them to remember his chains.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 4
s: Paul asks for prayer that God would open a door for the word so he can speak the mystery of Christ, for which he is in bonds. He sends Tychicus and Onesimus, relays greetings from his companions, instructs that the letter be shared with the Laodiceans, and writes the closing greeting in his own hand, asking the recipients to remember his chains.

l: Tychicus, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 4
s: Tychicus is described as a beloved brother, faithful servant and fellow bondservant in the Lord. Paul sends him to the recipients to make known all his affairs, to learn their circumstances and to comfort their hearts.

l: Onesimus, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 4
s: Onesimus is called a faithful and beloved brother who is one of the recipients' own. He is sent with Tychicus to tell them everything going on where Paul is.

l: Epaphras, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 4
s: Epaphras, described as one of the recipients' own and a servant of Christ, sends greetings. He is always striving for them in prayer that they may stand perfect and complete in all God's will, and Paul testifies that he has great zeal for them and for those in Laodicea and Hierapolis.

l: recipients of the letter (Colossians), Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 4
s: The recipients are exhorted to treat servants justly if they are masters, to continue steadfastly in prayer with thanksgiving, to walk wisely toward outsiders and to speak graciously. They are told to expect Tychicus and Onesimus, to greet the brothers in Laodicea with Nymphas and the assembly in his house, to read this letter also to the Laodiceans and read the one from Laodicea, and to tell Archippus to fulfill his ministry.

l: this letter, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, Chapter 4
s: The letter ends with greetings from Paul's companions and Paul's own handwritten greeting. It is to be read among the recipients and then also in the assembly of the Laodiceans, who are in turn to share a letter from Laodicea with them.

l: 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: Paul, an apostle, writes to Timothy, his true child in the faith, greeting him with grace, mercy, and peace. He reminds Timothy to stay at Ephesus and command certain men not to teach a different doctrine or follow myths and endless genealogies. Paul says the goal of the command is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith, and that some have turned to vain talking as would-be teachers of the law, which is good when used lawfully. Paul thanks Christ Jesus for appointing him to service despite his past as a blasphemer and persecutor, calling himself the chief of sinners who obtained mercy as an example to future believers. He charges Timothy to wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience, and names Hymenaeus and Alexander as men who shipwrecked their faith and whom he delivered to Satan so they might learn not to blaspheme.

l: Paul, 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: Paul introduces himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God and writes to Timothy. He recalls urging Timothy to stay at Ephesus, thanks Christ for counting him faithful and appointing him to service, and calls himself the chief of sinners who obtained mercy despite having been a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent. He also reports that he delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan so they might be taught not to blaspheme.

l: Timothy, 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: Timothy is addressed as Paul's true child in faith and is told to stay at Ephesus to command certain men not to teach a different doctrine. Paul commits this instruction to him according to earlier prophecies, so that he may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience.

l: Christ Jesus, 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is called our hope and Lord, and is named alongside God as the source of grace, mercy, and peace. He enabled Paul, counted him faithful, and appointed him to service. The text says he came into the world to save sinners and displayed all his patience in Paul as an example to those who would believe in him for eternal life.

l: God, 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: God is called our Savior and Father, and his commandment is the basis of Paul's apostleship. He is praised as the King eternal, immortal, invisible, who alone is wise, worthy of honor and glory forever. The Good News is described as that of the glory of the blessed God, committed to Paul's trust.

l: Hymenaeus, 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: Hymenaeus is named as one of those who thrust away faith and a good conscience and made shipwreck concerning the faith. Paul delivered him to Satan so that he might be taught not to blaspheme.

l: Alexander, 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: Alexander is named alongside Hymenaeus as having made shipwreck concerning the faith. Paul delivered him to Satan that he might be taught not to blaspheme.

l: false teachers (at Ephesus), 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: Certain men at Ephesus teach a different doctrine and pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes rather than God's stewardship in faith. Having missed the mark, some have turned to vain talking, desiring to be teachers of the law while understanding neither what they say nor what they affirm. Timothy is to command them not to teach this way.

l: the law, 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: The law is said to be good if a person uses it lawfully. It is not made for the righteous but for the lawless, insubordinate, ungodly, sinners, unholy, and profane, and for others such as murderers, the sexually immoral, slave-traders, liars, and perjurers, and anything contrary to sound doctrine, in accordance with the Good News.

l: 1 Timothy, 1 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: The author urges that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, including kings and those in high places, so that believers may lead tranquil and godly lives. He grounds this in God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to know the truth, and in the one God and one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. The author states he was appointed preacher, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles. He then instructs men to pray everywhere with holy hands, without anger and doubting, and women to dress modestly and adorn themselves with good works. Finally, he says he does not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man, citing Adam being formed first and Eve being deceived, and says the woman will be saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love, and holiness with sobriety.

l: God, 1 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: God our Savior is said to find prayer for all people good and acceptable. He desires all people to be saved and to come to full knowledge of the truth, and he is the one God.

l: Christ Jesus, 1 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: Christ Jesus is identified as the one mediator between God and men, and as a man. He gave himself as a ransom for all, which is described as the testimony at the proper time.

l: Adam, 1 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: Adam is cited as having been formed first, before Eve. He is said not to have been deceived, which is used as part of the grounds for the restriction on women teaching.

l: Eve, 1 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: Eve is named as formed after Adam. The text says the woman, being deceived, fell into disobedience.
